newsitem.title: USA: Maine governor expected to sign budget.
newsitem.headline: Maine governor expected to sign budget.

text.p: Maine Gov. Angus King was expected Wednesday to sign a $3.8 billion budget pushed through the legislature by Democrats three months ahead of schedule.

The House and Senate gave final approval to the two-year spending package late Tuesday, rejecting Republican efforts to protect an income tax cap that had been scheduled to take effect at the end of the fiscal year June 30.
By having the budget approved before April 1, Democrats took advantage of a parlimentary rule that allowed the budget to be passed by a simple majority rather than a two-thirds marjority.
Democrats control both the House and Senate but not with a two-thirds majorities in either. Gov. King, an independent, had supported the Democrat's strategy.
"This is an end to hostage taking," said House Speaker Elizabeth Mitchell, citing Republican threats to shut down state government if the cap on income tax receipts were not allowed to take effect.
The tax cap, which would cut revenues by $131 million in the next two years, was put into the budget last year by Republicans, who declined then to identify where the spending cuts would be made.

King and Democratic leaders said the state could not afford to lose the revenue at this time. This budget includes $10 million for an income tax relief fund and $6 million to increase personal income tax exemptions.
Republicans scoffed at claims this budget offered tax relief, with Rep. David Ott accusing Democrats and King in debate Tuesday of believing in the Easter Bunny.
Republicans also accused Democrats of including several items -- including $500,000 to create a family court system -- without public hearings or proper debate.

Among the other items in the budget; $44.5 million to increase state aid to local schools; $11.6 million more for the university system; and $2 million to purchase Sears Island, the onetime proposed site of a cargo terminal.

The decision to approve the budget before April 1 means legislators will have to adjourn this session later this week but they will almost immediately be called back into special session to consider unfinished business.

Issues still to be considered by lawmakers include King's proposal to double the cigarette tax, bills to deregulate the electric industry and whether to enact a ban on same-sex marriages or put the measure to voters in November.
